summary: Some IS-IS TLVs need to carry more than the 255-byte limit allows. This document records the common mechanism of spreading the content across multiple TLVs.

eli5.summary: A short note cannot hold a long story, so you continue on more notes. This describes how the routing messages do that.

questions: what is a multi-part tlv in is-is
how do you send a tlv larger than 255 octets
what is is-is mp-tlv support sub-tlv
how do is-is routers combine multiple tlvs
subtitle: How IS-IS routers spread information that does not fit in a 255-octet TLV across several TLVs, and how receivers must put it back together.

tldr.problem: An IS-IS TLV has a one-octet Length, so it carries at most 255 octets, and growing networks and new features push many TLVs past that limit. Many TLV definitions never said whether a TLV may be repeated.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC makes repeating a TLV with the same type and key the standard way to extend it. Receivers that support these Multi-Part TLVs process all parts as if they were concatenated, and a new Router CAPABILITY sub-TLV (type 30) tells operators which routers support it.
tldr.outcome: It is now the default extension mechanism for future TLVs. IANA registries gained an MP column saying where it applies, and operators are told to enable sending only when every receiving router can handle it.

facts.label: Extended IS reachability key
facts.value: 7 octets system ID and pseudonode number, plus link identifiers

today: RFC 9885 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The 255-Octet Limit
sections.content:
IS-IS routers describe themselves and their links with TLVs: Type-Length-Value tuples. Both Type and Length are one octet, so a TLV holds at most 255 octets of payload. Growing networks and new traffic engineering attributes make that limit a real problem.

Some TLV definitions already say a TLV may appear several times in a Link State PDU, but many do not. For example, RFC 5305 defines the Extended IS reachability TLV (22) and RFC 5120 defines the MT-ISN TLV (222), and neither describes sending multiple TLVs for the same object.

This RFC states plainly that multiple occurrences of a TLV are the standard way to scale TLV contents. Any future document proposing another mechanism for a codepoint must explain why repeating the TLV is not appropriate. The mechanism applies to top-level TLVs and to sub-TLVs at any level. Encodings that already allow repeats, such as the Router CAPABILITY TLV (242), are not changed.
sections.eli5: A small box only holds so much. Rather than inventing a bigger box, everyone agrees that you can use several small boxes with the same label.

sections.title: Keys and Multi-Part TLVs
sections.content:
Two kinds of TLV benefit. Some are simply a list of objects, like the BFD-Enabled TLV (148) listing pairs of identifiers. Others advertise objects that each have a unique set of identifiers, called the key.

For the Extended IS reachability TLV (22), the key is the 7 octets of system ID and pseudonode number plus the link identifiers present. For the Extended IP reachability TLV (135), the key is the 6 bits of prefix length plus 0 to 4 octets of IPv4 prefix.

If a router sends several TLVs with the same type and the same key in a Hello packet or in the set of LSPs for a level, they form a Multi-Part TLV (MP-TLV). The encoding does not change and the key is whatever the TLV's own specification defines. The RFC deliberately does not list keys for every codepoint.

Each part MUST be parsable on its own. A sub-TLV or other data unit MUST NOT be split across parts.
sections.eli5: Cards that share a title and a name tag belong to the same story. Each card must make sense by itself, so you may not cut a sentence in half between two cards.

sections.title: How Receivers Handle the Parts
sections.content:
A router that receives an MP-TLV MUST accept all the information in all the parts. Order and placement do not matter: parts MAY be in one LSP or in different LSPs, and their position in a Hello is irrelevant. Without MP-TLV support, the receiver picks one TLV to process and ignores the others.

Receivers MUST NOT impose a minimum length check. Senders SHOULD NOT split unless the 255-octet capacity is exceeded, but receivers MUST NOT reject MP-TLVs when they do, even if two parts of 100 bytes each add up to less than 255.

The contents are processed as if concatenated. If one part has key K with sub-TLVs A, B and C and another has key K with D, E and F, the receiver sees key K with A through F in any order.

Conflicts are errors. Different values in the fixed part that is not the key, or a once-only sub-TLV that appears twice with different values, are examples. If the TLV's own document is silent, the first occurrence in the lowest numbered LSP is used and later ones are ignored; in a Hello, the first occurrence is used.
sections.eli5: When you get several cards, read them all and treat them as one long story. If two cards disagree, trust the first one you find.

sections.title: Where MP-TLV Applies
sections.content:
MP-TLV procedures are potentially applicable to any codepoint that allows sub-TLVs, and to codepoints that define an unbounded number of attributes, such as GMPLS-SRLG (RFC 5307). Because specifications were silent, interoperability problems are likely when more than 255 octets must be sent.

To fix this, IANA added an MP column to the relevant IS-IS registries. The initial values follow one rule: MP-TLV is applicable (Y) to any codepoint that supports sub-TLVs, whether or not current sub-TLVs would actually need it. Future codepoints must state applicability explicitly.
sections.eli5: Each kind of card now has a checkbox saying 'you may continue this one on more cards, yes or no'.

sections.title: Capability Advertisement and Deployment
sections.content:
Turning on MP-TLV where specifications never defined it can be very disruptive if some routers do not support it. A router that ignores some parts of a neighbor advertisement could compute wrong constrained paths, causing forwarding loops or dropped traffic.

To help operators, a new sub-TLV of the Router CAPABILITY TLV (RFC 7981) is defined: MP-TLV Support for TLVs with Implicit Support, Type 30, Length 0. Routers with such support SHOULD include it, at per-level scope. It is informational only: implementations MUST NOT change what they send or how they process what they receive because of it. It has no per-codepoint syntax.

Implementations that send MP-TLVs are RECOMMENDED to provide configuration controls to enable or disable generation, ideally per codepoint. If disablement is supported, they MUST log when an MP-TLV is received while disabled, and when local LSP generation needs MP-TLVs while disabled. Operators SHOULD NOT enable MP-TLVs until all receivers can interpret them.

Senders SHOULD NOT use multiple TLVs unless MP-TLV applies and the information exceeds one TLV. If there is no room in the current LSP, the TLV SHOULD be moved to a new LSP.
sections.eli5: Before you start using extra cards, check that everyone in the group knows how to read them, or some people will get the story wrong. There is also a sign that a router can hold up to say 'I can read extra cards'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it creates no new security issues for IS-IS and that additional instances of existing TLVs expose no new information. Support for MP-TLV may even make an implementation more robust when it meets an unexpected MP-TLV.

Security concerns for IS-IS are covered in ISO/IEC 10589, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310.
sections.eli5: Using more cards does not reveal any new secrets. The old safety rules stay the same.
